The data displays model-based projections for wheat yield for the baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) periods under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 (in Tons/ha). This data is an output from the DSSAT (Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer) model which simulates growth, development and yield of a crop growing on a uniform area of land under prescribed or simulated management as well as the changes in soil water, carbon, and nitrogen that take place under the cropping system over time. The main factors affecting crop yield include air temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, wind speed, water availability, and atmospheric CO2 concentration. Increase in temperature adversely affects crop physiology and results in decreasing crop yields and grain quality. Increase in atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide may lead to increase plant growth of certain crops. DSSAT can be used at a farm level to determine the impact of climate change on crop production and potential adaptation practices that should be developed for farmers. DSSAT outputs can be used in economic models which are designed to estimate the potential impacts of climate change on production, consumption, income, gross domestic product (GDP), employment, and farm value. The Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group monthly climate normals are baseline data sets describing average monthly conditions over the most recent three full decades. The most recent PRISM normals are for the period 1981-2010. Spatial climate data sets for mean monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature were developed for the conterminous United States. These 30-arcsec (∼800-m) grids are the official spatial climate data sets of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The PRISM interpolation method was used to develop data sets that reflected, as closely as possible, the current state of knowledge of spatial climate patterns in the United States. PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each digital elevation model (DEM) grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell. Factors considered are location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position, and orographic effectiveness of the terrain. Surface stations used in the analysis numbered nearly 13,000 for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature. Station data were spatially quality controlled, and short-period-of-record averages adjusted to better reflect the 1981–2010 period.

The data represents annual change in the surface runoff for baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 emission scenarios in millimetre (mm). This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds. Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics. The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include: • Precipitation. • Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow. • Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET). • Base flow. • Ground water recharge. The Human Impacts on Oceans data set identifies the areas of the oceans that are most- and least- impacted by human stressors. This 5 km resolution global map was created by Stanford University (Stanford), Imperial College London (Imperial), and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB). This study considered 20 ocean ecosystem types and 19 stressors. The 19 stressors considered were artisanal fishing, 5 types of commercial fishing (pelagic vs. demersal, high vs. lowbycatch, destructive of habitat vs. nondestructive), commercial shipping, inorganic pollution, organic pollution, nutrient pollution, ocean-based pollution, light pollution, invasive species, 4 climate-change stressors (warming, acidification, sea-level rise, UV changes), direct human use, and oil rigs. Stressor inputs into the model come from data sets for years ranging from 1981 to 2013. The sensitivity of each ecosystem type to each stressor was determined by surveying 135 experts from 19 countries, and these sensitivities were used to weight the impacts of the stressors in different areas of the ocean. Modeling the vulnerability of ecosystems is challenging for many reasons. Ecosystem response to different stressors is often simplified for model development and the combined effects of multiple stressors on an ecosystem are not always well-understood. Additionally, relevant data may be missing or contain errors. Ignoring this uncertainty can lead to poor ocean management decisions. This map identifies regions of the oceans with high and low human impacts that were robust to these uncertainties, meaning that these areas were identified as being highly or minimally impacted by humans in simulations run over a range of plausible ecological conditions. Seven different factors of uncertainty were tested in 3000 simulations, each of which produced a map of the human impact on different parts of the ocean. Within each map, the 25% of ocean areas with the highest and lowest human impacts, respectively, were identified. The number of times each grid cell was categorized as a high-impact area or a low-impact area was counted. This map shows grid cells that were identified in each category in 75-90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Likely) and in over 90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Very Likely). ### Overview The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the First Theme, Land and Water Resources, is displayed here and allows for the uniform classification of [biophysical](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/biophysics) resources that are relevant for agricultural production systems. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. ​​Information on the current and future use of land resources is important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on the biophysical limitations of land, current crop suitability, and information on how different agricultural resources may be impacted by climate change. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change. ### Methodology Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data for AEZ is derived from climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps. The Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) sub-theme outputs fall under the first Theme, Land and Water Resources, and provides an inventory of land resources for the assessment of land productivity under specific agro-ecological conditions. Thermal and moisture layers are combined with broad categories of soil and terrain qualities allowing for the identification of land areas with biophysical constraints. A rigorous methodology and set of explicit principles are followed to assemble the AEZ classes and definitions. The following principles ensure that: 1) the map classes align with major climate zones based on the baseline historical period of 1981-2010, 2) map classes reflect broad ranges of the length of growing period boundaries, and 3) AEZ classes have generalized information about the prevailing soil and terrain limitations that are derived from GAEZ v4 terrain and soil resources inventories. The final AEZ layer has 57 different classes that are mapped at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Agro-Ecological Zones data has additional data for 2071-2100 and additional RCPs (2.6 and 6). For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. The third edition of the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set - Heliosat (SARAH-3) is a satellite-based climate data record of the solar surface irradiance (SIS), the surface direct irradiance ((direct horizontal and direct normalized, SID and DNI), the sunshine duration (SDU), the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), daylight (DAL), and the effective cloud albedo derived (CAL) from satellite-observations of the visible channels of the MVIRI and the SEVIRI instruments onboard the geostationary Meteosat satellites. SARAH-3 covers the time period 1 Jan 1983 - 31 Dec 2020 as climate data record (CDR) and is operationally extended as Interim Climate Data Record (ICDR) to the present with a latency of 5 days; the data cover the region ±65° longitude and ±65° latitude. The products are available as monthly (P1M) and daily (P1D) means, and as 30-min instantaneous data (PT30M) (sunshine duration is available as monthly and daily sum) on a regular latitude/longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.05° x 0.05° degrees. The data record is complemented with a comprehensive documentation of the algorithms used and the generation of the data record. Validation report and user guidance are also available. All product are available via the CM SAF Web User Interface. The daily and monthly mean surface incoming shortwave radiation (SIS) and the daily and monthly sums of sunshine duration (SDU) are also provided via EUMETCast. Note: the CDR coverage ends on the 31/12/2020. Dates after 31/12/2020 are covered by the ICDR.

description: Purpose To provide a high-resolution, longitudinal global data set of extreme urban heat events and urban heat exposure. Abstract The Global High Resolution Daily Extreme Urban Heat Exposure (UHE-Daily), 1983-2016 data set contains a high-resolution, longitudinal global record of geolocated urban extreme heat events and urban population exposure estimates for more than 10,000 urban settlements worldwide for 1983-2016. Urban extreme heat events and urban population exposure are identified for each urban settlement in the data record for five combined temperature-humidity thresholds: two-day or longer periods where the daily maximum Heat Index (HImax) > 40.6 °C; one-day or longer periods where HImax > 46.1 °C; and one day or longer periods where the daily maximum Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGTmax) > 28 °C, 30 °C, and 32 °C. The WBGTmax thresholds follow the International Standards Organization (ISO) criteria for risk of occupational heat related heat illness, whereas the HImax thresholds follow the U.S. National Weather Services' definition for an excessive heat warning. For each criteria, across urban settlements worldwide, the data set also contains the duration, intensity, and severity of each urban extreme heat event. Documentation To access the documentation of this resource, you can use the following link: https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/sdei-high-res-daily-uhe-1983-2016/docs Download To download this dataset, you can use the following link (Login required): https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/sdei-high-res-daily-uhe-1983-2016/data-download Related materials This resource is associated with the Earth Observations Toolkit for Sustainable Cities and Human Settlements. If you want to learn more about it, please, check the EO Toolkit portal (https://eotoolkit.unhabitat.org/), a place where you will find use cases, learning material, and many other tools and resources related to the Sustainable Development Goal 11 and New Urban Agenda.

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](79f16b9a-a062-4820-822d-7858609a8fd5) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview This dataset shows the locations of seasonal water and permanent water for each year between 1984 and 2018. A permanent water surface is an area that is underwater for all 12 months of the year, while a seasonal water surface is underwater for less than 12 months of the year. This dataset has a 30 meter resolution. Water is essential for Earth’s plant and animal life, as well as for many human activities. Surface water also affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between Earth’s surface and atmosphere. The dataset can be used to support sectors such as water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. This data is a part of the Global Surface Water dataset, created by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center. ### Methodology Water coverage was detected using satellite imagery from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 that was collected between 1984 and 2018. To detect water, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques such as expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. An expert system is a classification process that can account for data uncertainty and incorporate image interpretation expertise. In some places, observations for all 12 months of the year were not available. For example, some parts of the world experience a polar night during parts of the year, in which the night lasts for more than 24 hours. These areas do not have adequate imagery to detect surface water coverage for all 12 months. In cases where 12 months of data was not available, water is considered to be permanent if the number of months where water is present is equal to the number of months where valid observations were acquired. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal. Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: ### Overview This dataset displays the global location and temporal distribution of water surfaces from 1984 to 2018 at a spatial resolution of 30 meters. The dataset includes individual layers of water occurrence, occurrence change intensity, seasonality, recurrence, and maximum water extent. Water occurrence is the frequency in which water was present on the surface. Occurrence change intensity shows where surface water occurrence increased, decreased or remained the same across the 35 years. Seasonality suggests the difference between permanent and seasonal water and the number of months water was present. Recurrence displays the changes in surface water classes. Maximum water extent provides information on all the locations ever detected as water over the 35 year period. The dataset was created using a combination of Landsat 5, 7, and 8 satellite imagery that was analyzed using a variety of information extraction techniques. The dataset was tested and found to have less than 1% error. Surface water affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between the earth’s surface and atmosphere. Water is essential for plants, animals, and human activities. The dataset was commissioned by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center to support water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. Understanding Earth’s water will continue to grow in importance as world temperature and human population rises. ### Methodology This dataset used a combination of Landsat satellite imagery. Data from Landsat 5 Thematic Mapper, Landsat 7 Enhanced Thematic Mapper-plus, and Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager were analyzed for the period of 1984 to 2018. The satellite imagery was corrected for top-of-atmosphere reflectance and brightness temperature images. Information from the Global Human Settlement Data Layer (GHSL) was used to determine the location of buildings and correct the final map for interference from their shadows. Due to the difficulty of using satellite imagery to detect water across geography and temporality, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques to analyze the remote imaging data. Researchers largely relied on a series of expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. The expert system classified each image pixel into one of three categories: water, land, or non-valid observations (unusable data). It used both multispectral and multitemporal attributes from Landsat images and was created using a string of If-Then rules to create a reliable line of reasoning. . Visual analytics were used to verify the accuracy of the categories determined in the expert system and to create an equation to help describe pixel clusters of different categories. Lastly, evidential reasoning assisted in guiding class assignments in the expert system. It used geographic location and temporal trajectory to delineate boundaries of often misinterpreted areas, like glaciers and lava flows. The final dataset was created using raster format at a spatial resolution of 30 meters. For the full documentation about calculation for individual layers, please see the source [publication](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal. Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly recurrence and monthly water history are available from the data provider. description: The anomalies of three basic-ECVs have been created: daily maximum near surface air temperature (tasmax), precipitation (pr) and near surface wind speed (sfcWind). The anomalies have been generated using the basic ECVs to offer additional relevant information for the quantification of climate hazards. These maps are created using the basic-ecvs in raster format with a spatial resolution of 5.5 km (1 km for Azores) obtained by statistically downscaling a set of CMIP6 simulations for different IPCC climate scenarios (historical, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5) and 30-year average time periods (historical, short time-period, medium time-period, long time-period). For the anomaly calculation, the historical period (1985-2014) layer of each ECV and CS has been assumed as the reference 30-year average values. While the daily maximum near surface air temperature and near surface wind speed variables are represented in °C and m/s, respectively; precipitation is displayed as percentage. This repository includes the products in geotiff format, the styles in sld format, the derived maps in jpg and the metadata files in xml.

description: ### Overview The Flood Events dataset shows major flood events within the last month. This near real-time dataset is created using data from news articles and government sources. While the map only shows the location and extent for floods within the last month, additional information on flood start and end dates, number of deaths, number of people displaced, main cause, and severity are all available in the Custom Visualization tool below. According to the [United Nations](https://www.unenvironment.org/news-and-stories/story/how-climate-change-making-record-breaking-floods-new-normal), floods will become more likely due to global climate change. They can have large consequences for civil society including the loss of life, damage to property, and increasing health risks. This dataset lets viewers monitor where flooding is happening around the world on a near real-time basis. It can also offer a first glance at the communities that have been impacted by flooding. Lastly, it can help government agencies in creating natural disaster management plans and zoning for future urbanization. This dataset was created and is curated by the Dartmouth Flood Observatory located at the University of Colorado’s Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research (INSTAAR). It is a continually updated archive that can show trends in severity, damage, and location of flood events. ### Methodology This dataset was created and is continually updated with information from a wide array of news and government sources, like the North American Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration’s National Climatic Data Center (NOAA NCDC). To identify each flood, researchers used the international [Global Identified Number](https://glidenumber.net/glide/public/search/search.jsp) (GLIDE), which is a unique ID code used to identify disasters that is issued by the [Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT)](https://www.emdat.be/) at the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED). For each flood, event data on location, size, begin & end times, duration, deaths, number of people displaced, main cause, and severity were recorded. Size, times, duration, main cause, and location are all taken directly from the source. Number of deaths were taken from news and government sources when accurate enough, but when only a range of numbers were provided by these sources researchers estimated that “hundreds” meant more than 300 people had died, “more than 100” meant 110 or more had died, and “scores” meant more than 30 people had died. Number of people displaced was based on the quantity of people left homeless after the incident and sometimes the number evacuated during the flood. Severity was determined by reviewing the amount of damage caused by the event and how often similar events have occured in the region. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://floodobservatory.colorado.edu/Archives/ArchiveNotes.html). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Data on flood events for every year between 1985 and present are available from the data provider. Additionally, the data provider also has datasets on river and reservoir discharge, flood and drought-affected watersheds, and precipitation. An interactive map can also be found on the source website. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/wat_040_flood_events) ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The dataset shows up-to-date status, trends, and alerts related to sea surface temperature anomalies, which have the potential to cause bleaching where coral are present. Sea surface temperature (SST) is the water temperature close to the ocean's surface. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Coral Reef Watch (CRW) program has developed a daily global 5 kilometer (km) product suite based on satellite observations to monitor SST and thermal stress on coral reefs. Mass coral bleaching events due to anomalously warm ocean water have increased in frequency and severity and have become one of the most significant contributors to the deterioration of the world’s coral reefs. Thermal stress that persists for several weeks with ambient water temperatures as little as 1 to 2 degrees Celsius (°C) above a coral’s thermal tolerance level has been shown to cause bleaching, often on broad geographical scales. Corals can die if thermal stress is severe or long-lasting; furthermore, coral weakened by thermal stress may subsequently succumb to disease. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, reductions in fish productivity, and economic loss. Corals are capable of rebounding from bleaching, but not if the heat stress events are too severe or recur too quickly to permit recovery. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. Reliable global monitoring and prediction of environmental conditions leading to bleaching is used to guide targeted observations and management responses. The NOAA CRW products fulfill requests from coral reef managers and researchers for higher resolution products by taking advantage of new satellites, sensors and algorithms. ### Methodology The Coral Bleaching Monitoring dataset draws its layers from Version 3.1 of NOAA Coral Reef Watch’s experimental [coral bleaching heat stress monitoring product suite](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php). This product suite spans January 1, 1985 to present and is derived from CRW's Version 3.1 daily global 5 km satellite sea surface temperature (SST) data product known as ['CoralTemp'](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php). The Version 3.1 product suite was developed based on user requests and in order to address errors that were identified in the source SST data for CRW's Version 3.0 products for some coral reef regions during 2013-2016. It now comprises the core of CRW's Decision Support System (DSS) for coral reef management, providing service at or near reef-scales, allowing direct monitoring of 95% of global coral reefs and significantly reducing data gaps caused by cloud cover. Note that SST variability is often considerably higher at the much finer 5 km spatial and daily temporal resolutions, when compared with CRW's heritage twice-weekly global 50 km (0.5 degree) monitoring products. Due to resulting day-to-day fluctuations between stress levels in highly variable locations, the single-day 5 km Bleaching Alert Area product does not consistently and adequately identify potentially harmful heat stress levels, especially with regard to accumulated heat stress impacts. Rather than requiring users to examine the single-day 5 km Bleaching Alert Area product over several days, a 7-day maximum Bleaching Alert Area composite product, updated daily, was introduced in the Version 2 product suite and is maintained here in Version 3.1. The evolution of CRW's daily global 5 km product suites can be found [here](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/history_5km_products.php). This 7-day composite product shows the maximum stress level that a satellite pixel has experienced during the most recent seven consecutive days. Data and images are dated on the last day of the 7-day period. Notably, it is compatible with CRW's heritage twice-weekly global 50 km Bleaching Alert Area product, as the 50 km Bleaching Alert Area is based on a half-week (3 or 4 days) composite of 50 km SSTs (but with much less SST variability due to its much coarser spatial resolution). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data about heat stress frequency, heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. CRW's first-generation (heritage) near real-time [twice-weekly global 50 km satellite coral bleaching heat stress monitoring products](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/50km/) were operational at NOAA until April 30, 2020, when they were officially retired, and succeeded by CRW's next-generation operational daily global 5 km coral bleaching heat stress monitoring products. The heritage 50 km products served the U.S. and international coral reef communities for more than 20 years (1997-2020). While the 50km products no longer update in near real-time, due to their retirement, since they served as vital tools for our users for so many years, [archived 50km data and images](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/50km/) are still available on the CRW website. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/ocn_007_coral_bleaching_monitoring). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: ### Overview This dataset shows the frequency and intensity of heat stress events. Heat stress events can be detected using sea surface temperature (SST), which is the water temperature close to the ocean's surface. A heat stress event occurs when the SST near coral reefs exceeds the historical baseline for that area. This dataset describes the number of heat stress events and the average period of time between them during 1985-2018 at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. Stress events are defined by applying Coral Reef Watch's [Degree Heating Week (DHW) methodology] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/education/tutorial/crw24_dhw_product.php) at coral reef-containing and adjacent satellite pixel locations worldwide. The DHW attempts to capture both the level of abnormal heating and its duration: 1 DHW is equivalent to 1 week of SST 1°C above the expected summertime maximum at a given location. The three thresholds for heat stress in this dataset correspond to occurrence (DHW>0), significant coral bleaching (DHW≥4), and widespread bleaching and significant mortality (DHW≥8). SST and its fluctuations are critical to ecosystem dynamics and health, as many marine organisms can thrive only within certain temperature ranges. In particular, research indicates that a coral reef’s “thermal history” is among the most important factors influencing its ability to withstand heat stress events. Accordingly, with support from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) [Coral Reef Conservation Program](http://coralreef.noaa.gov/), [Coral Reef Watch (CRW)] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php) developed a variety of thermal history metrics for coral reef management, initially released in July 2014. The metrics were derived from CRW's Version 3.1 [CoralTemp daily global 5 km (1/20°) satellite SST data product] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), for the period 1985-2018. Coral reef sites that have experienced fewer heat stress events may have natural protection from exposure to conditions conducive to bleaching (e.g., strong mixing, upwelling). However, corals at those sites may also be more sensitive to heat stress, resulting in higher impacts if a stress event does occur. Alternatively, sites that have been regularly exposed to heat stress can have a reduced sensitivity, and therefore lower impact from the stress. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. ### Methodology Stress events are defined for 1985-2018 by applying CRW's Degree Heating Week (DHW) methodology at pixel locations worldwide that either contained coral reefs or were adjacent to pixels that did. SST input data were drawn from the [CoralTemp daily global 5 km satellite SST data product (Version 3.1)](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), which represents the nighttime ocean temperature measured at the surface. The source data for CoralTemp are a combination of the: 1. NOAA/National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) operational near real-time daily global 5 km Geostationary-Polar-orbiting (Geo-Polar) Blended Night-only SST Analysis; 2. NOAA/NESDIS 2002-2016 reprocessed daily global 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-only SST Analysis; and the 3. 1985-2002 daily global 5 km night-only SST reanalysis produced by the United Kingdom Met Office, on the Operational SST and Sea Ice Analysis (OSTIA) system. NOAA's daily global 5 km Geostationary-Polar Blended Night-only SST Analyses (both the near real-time and reprocessed products) utilize sensors from multiple geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites to derive a global SST data field at a resolution of 5 km (1/20°). The few remaining gaps are filled using optimal interpolation through space and time. Heat stress will build up if the temperature around corals rises and stays above the bleaching threshold (1°C above the highest summertime mean SST). The DHW is the product of the deviation above this threshold and the length of time it persists. This captures not only how far the temperature is above the threshold, but how long it has stayed above that point. Thus the DHW shows how much heat stress has accumulated in an area over the past 12 weeks. It is a running sum: as time advances one half-week (a timestep), a half-week timestep "falls off" the back end of the 12-week window. Additional data about heat stress frequency, heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. description: ### Overview This dataset describes historical variations in sea surface temperature wherever coral reefs are present. Sea surface temperature (SST) is water temperature close to the ocean's surface. This changes everywhere within and between years, and the pattern and range of those fluctuations differ from place to place. This dataset characterizes those spatially distinct patterns at coral reef sites around the globe, by capturing the average variation in temperature from year to year in each 5 km grid cell, as well as the average variation in temperature from summer to summer (i.e., from the warmest month in each year to the next). SST and its fluctuations are critical to ecosystem dynamics and health, as many marine organisms can thrive only within certain temperature ranges. In particular, research indicates that thermal history is among the most important factors influencing coral reef resilience—i.e., ability to withstand heat stress events. Accordingly, with support from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) [Coral Reef Conservation Program](http://coralreef.noaa.gov/), [Coral Reef Watch (CRW)] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php) developed a variety of thermal history metrics for coral reef management, initially released in July 2014. The metrics were derived from CRW's Version 3.1 [CoralTemp daily global 5 km (1/20°) satellite SST data product] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), for the period 1985-2018. Historical SST variability has been related to the level of sensitivity of corals to heat stress, in that higher variability can confer lower sensitivity. Less-sensitive corals and reef sites are less impacted when exposed to particular heat stress levels. Annual variability speaks to the variability between years, which can modify the impact of heat stress events and the susceptibility of corals and reef sites to future events. Similarly, sites with high summer temperature variability can have less sensitivity to coral bleaching. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. ### Methodology Variability products are derived from the Version 3.1 [CoralTemp](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php) daily global 5km satellite SST data product. For the Annual Variability metric, the average temperature was determined for each year in the time-series (1985-2018). The warmest month was identified separately on the basis of a 28-year (1985-2012) record. The average temperature for the relevant period of time—either the entire year or the warmest month—is calculated for each year in the time-series (1985-2018); the variability shown is the standard deviation of these values after the removal of any linear trend. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data about heat stress frequency are also available for display here, while heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. description: ### Overview The Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents dataset shows the location of selected incidents that have occured from 1957 to present. The dataset shown on Resource Watch includes oil spills, chemical spills, and other incidents in which the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Office of Response and Restoration (OR&R) has been active in assisting with the incident response. The dataset includes United States waters and some international locations show as point locations. OR&R is the federal U.S. government organization with expertise in preparing for, evaluating, and responding to threats to coastal environments, including oil and chemical spills, releases from hazardous waste sites, and marine debris. They are responsible for responding to and providing scientific support to federal on-scene coordinators for these incidents. The dataset is intended to provide public access to the history of incidents that have occured. It can be used to show trends and the long term effects of spills. ### Methodology The Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents dataset was created by using data from reports created by NOAA's Office of Response and Restoration (OR&R). These reports are present for all oil, chemical, and other incidents that OR&R provided scientific support for. From each report the name, date, location (longitude/latitude), type of threat, and a brief description were cataloged in the Raw Incident dataset. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview This dataset from Global BRT Data shows cities that have active bus rapid transit (BRT) systems and the year in which they commenced. Global BRT Data collects information on BRT and bus priority systems in cities around the world. BRT systems are characterized by median-aligned and segregated bus lanes, preboard fare collection, and platform-level boarding. Bus priority systems are similar in that they include dedicated bus lanes, but they may not include all of the features necessary to be classified as a BRT system. The Bus Rapid Transit Locations dataset is managed and updated monthly by the World Resources Institute (WRI) Brazil Ross Center for Sustainable Cities. The dataset covers 171 cities globally from 1968 to 2019. ### Methodology The Bus Rapid Transit dataset was created by Global BRT Data. The data is collected and aggregated from various sources, including transit agencies or associations of transit agencies, government, researchers, and nongovernmental organizations. The data may be collected from websites, publications, conversations with experts, or direct observations. In instances where sources of published data contradict each other, Global BRT Data defers to data from transit agencies, governments, or peer-reviewed publications. The most current data available is used whenever possible. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP) was created by NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) and is now run by NOAA's Earth System Research Laboratory Physical Sciences Division (ESRL-PSD). GISTEMP provides an estimate of global surface and air temperature changes. The basic GISS temperature analysis scheme was defined by James Hansen in the late 1970s, when a method of estimating global temperature change was needed for comparison with 1-dimensional global climate models. The scheme was based on the finding that the correlation of temperature change was reasonably strong for stations separated by up to 1,200 km, especially at middle and high latitudes. This fact proved sufficient to obtain useful estimates for global mean temperature changes. The analysis method was fully documented in Hansen and Lebedeff (1987), including quantitative estimates of the error in annual and 5-year mean temperature change. This was done by sampling at station locations a spatially complete data set of a long run of a global climate model, which was shown to have realistic spatial and temporal variability. This however only addresses the error due to incomplete spatial coverage of measurements. As there are other potential sources of error, such as urban warming near meteorological stations, many other methods have been used to verify the approximate magnitude of inferred global warming. These methods include inference of surface temperature change from vertical temperature profiles in the ground (bore holes) at many sites around the world, rate of glacier retreat at many locations, and studies by several groups of the effect of urban and other local human influences on the global temperature record. All of these yield consistent estimates of the approximate magnitude of global warming, which reached about 0.8°C in 2010, twice the magnitude reported in 1981. Further affirmation of the reality of the warming is its spatial distribution, which has largest values at locations remote from any local human influence, with a global pattern consistent with that expected for response to global climate forcings (larger in the Northern Hemisphere than the Southern Hemisphere, larger at high latitudes than low latitudes, larger over land than over ocean). More recent documentation compares alternative analyses and addresses questions about perception and reality of global warming; various choices for the ocean data are tested; it is also shown that global temperature change is sensitive to estimated temperature change in polar regions, where observations are limited. A multiyear smoothing is applied to fully remove the annual cycle and improve information content in temperature graphs. Despite large year-to-year fluctuations associated with the El Niño-La Niña cycle of tropical ocean temperature, the conclusion could be drawn that global temperature continued to rise rapidly in the 21st century, new record heights being reached in every decade. One of the improvements—introduced in 1998—was the implementation of a method to address the problem of urban warming: The urban and periurban (i.e., other than rural) stations are adjusted so that their long-term trend matches that of the mean of neighboring rural stations. Urban stations without nearby rural stations are dropped. This preserves local short-term variability without affecting long-term trends. Originally, the classification of stations was based on population size near that station; the current analysis uses satellite-observed night-lights to determine which stations are located in urban and periurban areas. This data set shows tree cover regrowth for South America for the period 1987-2016. Tree cover height is estimated annually using Landsat satellite imagery calibrated with LIDAR data. ### Overview The Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends dataset shows the average annual change in crop yield from 1989-2008. Agricultural crop yield is the amount of crop harvested per area of land. It is used to measure a crop’s performance. This study used approximately 1.8 million agricultural census reports from 13,500 political units around the world to determine how crop yield changed over time. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes, which is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.” Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. In order to meet projected demand, [crop production needs to double by 2050](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2296#MOESM1532). Improving crop yield, instead of clearing new land for agriculture, is one of the preferred solutions. In many areas, yield is stagnant or has collapsed entirely. Understanding where improvement is most needed can guide new agricultural investments. It is also important to identify and continue improving yield of high-performing crops and regions. This dataset was produced by EarthStat, a collaboration between the Global Landscapes Initiative (GLI) at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment (LUGE) lab at the University of British Columbia (UBC). EarthStat’s mission is to provide data on the global food system to help others make science-based decisions. The GLI is a scientific initiative that develops and applies tools to characterize global land use and evaluate global agricultural supply and demand trends. The LUGE lab is a research group that studies links between land use, global environmental change, and food security. ### Methodology Approximately 1.8 million census reports were used to determine yield of the four crops for the years between 1989 and 2008. Crop yield is the ratio of production (kilograms) and harvested area (hectares). According to the UN’s [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)](http://www.fao.org/waicent/faostat/agricult/pr_ele-e.htm), production is the amount of crop harvested. The harvested area is the area from which the crop is gathered. National-level data used in this study was provided by the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home), who collects data from the member countries’ statistical offices. At the time of the study, the FAO had crop data for 226 nations. In addition to national-level data, the study also used subnational data for the 51 countries that account for more than 70% of global production/harvested area for each of the four crops. Data was available at the state/province level for all 51 countries and county/district/município/department level for an additional 17 countries. This data was collected from these countries’ agricultural and statistical bureaus. According to the data provider, studies have used linear regression to project future crop yields. As such, the annual crop yields in this study (one data point per year) were linearly regressed to calculate the average change in yield from 1989-2008. A linear regression is a line modeled to fit the shape of a group of data points. The slope of the line gives the rate of change–in this case, the average yield change over the observed period. This calculation was performed for each crop at each political unit. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0066428#pone.0066428.s017). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The energy sector is strongly exposed to climate variability and change, from shifts in wind and solar resources to changing heating and cooling demand. Planning a resilient energy system therefore requires indicators that translate climate conditions into sector-relevant quantities. The Energy Indicators application provides wind, solar and energy-demand indicators derived from DestinE Climate Digital Twin (Climate DT) model data, enabling users to assess how energy supply and demand conditions vary in space and time and how they may change under future climate scenarios. More information can be found in the Climate DT User Guide. The application provides indicators for the energy sector: capacity factors for different wind turbines, wind speed histograms, and high- and low-wind events, alongside energy-demand indicators (heating and cooling degree-days) and a solar demand indicator (photovoltaic potential). The indicators are derived from hourly Climate DT output and provided globally at kilometre-scale resolution. By deriving these indicators consistently from Climate DT simulations, the application supports the analysis of climate-driven trends in renewable energy resources and energy demand, aiding adaptation planning across the energy sector. More information can be found in the user guide https://platform.destine.eu/docs/climate-dt-user-guide/doc/index.html

description: Precipitation is an essential variable to assess the severity of many extreme weather events. As a first assessment, it might be sufficient to look at daily rainfall totals for a given region. However, an in-depth analysis requires local information on severity, affected area and statistical return times to enable the development of fitted adaptation strategies. HydroMet fulfils this need by providing information on the intensity, duration, spatial extent and return time of extreme precipitation events over Europe based on DestinE Climate DT model data. More information can be found in the [Climate DT user guide](https://platform.destine.eu/services/documents-and-api/doc/?service_name=climate-dt-user-guide). The extreme precipitation parameters produced by HydroMet are based on existing products of the German Meteorological Service (DWD): KOSTRA2020, the latest version of KOSTRA-DWD (Shehu et al., 2023), and CatRaRE, Catalogue of Radar-based heavy Rainfall Events (Lengfeld et al., 2021). KOSTRA is a coordinated effort across German Federal states to develop methods for evaluating precipitation extremes from gauge-based observations. The system, developed over three decades, provides data about precipitation levels, duration and the annual return interval. CatRaRE is a software package able to detect and define extreme rain events and, at the same time, generate a catalogue with meteorological and geographical information for each event. At DWD, it is applied to radar data. HydroMet combines both products for a consistent dataset on the climatological scale. Shehu, B., Willems, W., Stockel, H., Thiele, L.-B., & Haberlandt, U. (2023). Regionalisation of rainfall depth–duration–frequency curves with different data types in Germany. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 27(5), 1109–1132. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-27-1109-2023 Lengfeld, K., Walawender, E., Winterrath, T., & Becker, A. (2021). CatRaRE: A Catalogue of radar-based heavy rainfall events in Germany derived from 20 years of data. Meteorologische Zeitschrift, 30(6), 469–487. https://doi.org/10.1127/metz/2021/1088

Note: This Generation 1 Collection has been superseded by Generation 2 Simulation-level Collections The DestinE Digital Twin for Climate Change Adaptation (Climate DT) supports adaptation activities by providing innovative climate information on multi-decadal timescales, globally, at scales at which many impacts of climate change are observed. It combines cutting-edge global Earth-system models, impact-sector applications and observations into a unified framework to provide global climate projections and impact-sector information on multi-decadal timescales (1990 to ~2050), at very high spatial resolutions (5 to 10 km). The Climate DT represents the first ever attempt to operationalise the production of global multi-decadal climate projections, leveraging the world-leading supercomputing facilities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking along with some of the leading European climate models. A concise overview of what the Climate DT aims to achieve, and of the different concepts essential for an understanding of the Digital Twin’s characteristics, is included in the [Climate DT factsheet](https://destine.ecmwf.int/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024.06.07_Climate-DT-Fact-Sheet_V7-2.pdf) ## Historical Simulation Starting in 1990, the forcing follows observed changes in greenhouse gases, aerosols etc. until 2020. The simulations are using standardised CMIP6 forcing. Historical simulations are essential for model evaluation and quality control as they allow a comparison to observations. ## Models The Climate DT exploits and further evolves a new generation of global storm-resolving and eddy-rich models built through a cooperative model development approach. For more information on models please click [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#models) ## Simulations The Climate DT team carries out several types of digital twin simulations on the EuroHPC supercomputers. Multi-decadal simulations are produced to cover the recent past (from 1990) and possible future evolutions of the climate up to 2050. See [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#simulations) for more information on Simulations ## Parameters Below we see the list of parameters extracted from the 'DestinE Climate DT data portfolio', for more information please refer to the page [Climate DT Phase 1 CLTE Parameters](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DDCZ/Climate+DT+Phase+1+data+catalogue)

description: Note: This Generation 1 Collection has been superseded by Generation 2 Simulation-level Collections The nextGEMS data is aligned with the Climate Change Adaptation Digital Twin. The DestinE Digital Twin for Climate Change Adaptation (Climate DT) supports adaptation activities by providing innovative climate information on multi-decadal timescales, globally, at scales at which many impacts of climate change are observed. It combines cutting-edge global Earth-system models, impact-sector applications and observations into a unified framework to provide global climate projections and impact-sector information on multi-decadal timescales (1990 to ~2050), at very high spatial resolutions (5 to 10 km). The Climate DT represents the first ever attempt to operationalise the production of global multi-decadal climate projections, leveraging the world-leading supercomputing facilities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking along with some of the leading European climate models. A concise overview of what the Climate DT aims to achieve, and of the different concepts essential for an understanding of the Digital Twin’s characteristics, is included in the [Climate DT factsheet](https://destine.ecmwf.int/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024.06.07_Climate-DT-Fact-Sheet_V7-2.pdf) ## Historical Simulation Starting in 1990, the forcing follows observed changes in greenhouse gases, aerosols etc. until 2020. The simulations are using standardised CMIP6 forcing. Historical simulations are essential for model evaluation and quality control as they allow a comparison to observations. ## Models The Climate DT exploits and further evolves a new generation of global storm-resolving and eddy-rich models built through a cooperative model development approach. For more information on models please click [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#models) ## Simulations The Climate DT team carries out several types of digital twin simulations on the EuroHPC supercomputers. Multi-decadal simulations are produced to cover the recent past (from 1990) and possible future evolutions of the climate up to 2050. See [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#simulations) for more information on Simulations ## Parameters Below we see the list of parameters extracted from the 'DestinE Climate DT data portfolio', for more information please refer to the page [Climate DT Phase 1 CLTE Parameters](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DDCZ/Climate+DT+Phase+1+data+catalogue)

description: Wildfires are strongly influenced by weather and climate conditions, particularly prolonged drought, high temperatures, low humidity and strong winds. Assessing wildfire danger therefore requires indicators that combine the effects of multiple meteorological variables into a single measure of fire-conducive conditions. The Fire Weather Index (FWI, Van Wagner 1987; Wotton 2009) application fulfils this need by providing information on wildfire danger globally based on DestinE Climate Digital Twin (Climate DT) model data. The application enables users to assess the temporal evolution, spatial distribution and long-term changes of fire weather conditions and associated wildfire risk. More information can be found in the [User Guide](https://platform.destine.eu/docs/climate-dt-user-guide/doc/index.html). The FWI application is based on the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System, one of the most widely used operational wildfire danger rating systems worldwide. The system combines temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and precipitation to estimate the moisture content of different fuel layers and the potential behaviour of wildfires. The output includes the Fire Weather Index (FWI), which is calculated using the Fine Fuel Moisture Code (FFMC), Duff Moisture Code (DMC), Drought Code (DC), Initial Spread Index (ISI), and Buildup Index (BUI). Together, these components describe the likelihood of ignition, fuel availability, and potential fire intensity. By applying the Fire Weather Index System consistently to Climate DT simulations, the application provides a harmonized assessment of current and future fire weather conditions, enabling the analysis of extreme fire seasons, climate-driven trends in wildfire danger and regional differences in fire-prone environments across Europe. Van Wagner, C. E. (1987). Development and structure of the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System. Forestry Technical Report 35, Canadian Forestry Service. Wotton, B. M. (2009). Interpreting and using outputs from the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System in research applications. Environmental and Ecological Statistics, 16, 107-131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-007-0084-2

description: Land surface hydrology governs the availability of water for ecosystems, agriculture and human use, and its response to climate change is a key concern for adaptation planning. The HydroLand application provides land surface hydrology indicators, including soil moisture, discharge and aridity, derived from DestinE Climate Digital Twin (Climate DT) model data. The application enables users to assess the spatial distribution, seasonal variability and long-term changes of hydrological conditions. More information can be found in the Climate DT User Guide. HydroLand is based on the Mesoscale Hydrologic Model (mHM, mhm-ufz.org), a distributed hydrological model that simulates the terrestrial water cycle from meteorological forcing. mHM is driven by Climate DT output to produce fluxes such as river discharge, evapotranspiration and soil moisture, which are then processed into user-oriented indicators covering soil moisture, discharge, and aridity. The dataset also includes the original mHM outputs and figures documenting model validation and selected results. By applying mHM consistently to Climate DT simulations, the application provides a harmonised assessment of current and future hydrological conditions globally, supporting the analysis of drought, water availability and climate-driven trends in the terrestrial water cycle.

description: ### Overview The Gross Domestic Product Per Capita dataset shows gross domestic product (GDP) per person based on purchasing power parity (PPP), converted to international dollars. GDP is the sum of the value of all the goods and services produced within a nation in a given year. PPP equalizes each country’s purchasing power by controlling for differences in price levels between economies. An international dollar has the same purchasing power over GDP as the U.S. dollar has in the United States. In other words, an international dollar would buy a comparable amount of goods and services in any country that a U.S. dollar would buy in the United States. Data is shown for each year between 1990 and present at a national resolution. The World Bank Group International Comparison Program (World Bank Group ICP) estimates PPPs for the world’s economies in order to provide comparable price and volume measures of GDP. This dataset lets users compare national GDP between countries, currencies, and time. PPPs and underlying World Bank Group ICP data are utilized for a wide variety of analyses at the global, regional, and national levels and cover many themes under the economic, environmental, and social development umbrellas. They can be used not only by the development community and researchers, but by policymakers, the media, and the wider public. The World Bank Group ICP is one of the largest statistical initiatives in the world. It relies on a partnership of international, regional, sub-regional, and national agencies working under a robust governance framework and following an established statistical methodology. Its main objectives are to produce PPPs for participating countries and to convert GDP and its expenditure components into a common currency. ### Methodology The Gross Domestic Product Per Capita dataset has three major components for its methodology: - The System of National Accounts (SNA) definition of final expenditures on GDP - The basket of goods and services from which items are selected for pricing - The methodology used to compute PPPs, within and across regions The SNA uses national expenditures as weights to aggregate PPPs through the various levels of aggregation up to GDP. The basket of goods and services, also known as the global core list of items, is used to compare the same items between different countries within a region. The methodology used to compute PPPs is based on two approaches: the Jevons index by Gini-Éltető-Köves-Szulc (GEKS) and the country product dummy method. More in-depth information about these methods can be found in the World Bank Group ICP’s document on [Measuring the Real Size of the World Economy](http://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/927971487091799574/ICPBook-eBook-FINAL.pdf). Each participating economy also provides the following required data: - National annual average prices for a selection of items chosen from a common basket - A breakdown of national expenditures in local currency according to a common classification - Market exchange rates - Population The national average prices and national expenditures are used to calculate PPPs and are reported by participating economies in their local currencies. Both cover the whole range of final goods and services constituting the GDP. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/icp#6). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows data from the World Bank Group ICP for [Gross Domestic Product (PPP, Current International $)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Gross-Domestic-Product). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The data provider has additional data on gross domestic product separated into 44 expenditure headings, national accounts expenditures in PPP, and price level indices available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of the population with access to electricity from 1990 to present, at the country level. The data represents electricity access in the urban population of each country. Access to electricity is crucial to improving the standard of living and is one of the most obvious indications of a country’s energy poverty status. Securing electricity services while decarbonizing power systems is a key challenge for developing countries, as electricity generation from fossil fuels contributes to climate change. While this dataset shows access to electricity at the national level, Resource Watch also shows data for the percentage of [rural](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012b-Access-to-Electricity-Rural) and [national](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012a-Access-to-Electricity) population with access to electricity. This dataset comes from a Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) database from the SE4ALL Global Tracking Framework led jointly by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). ### Methodology Electrification data is collected from industry, national surveys, and international sources. Data generally comes from nationally representative household surveys like national censuses. Survey sources include Demographic and Health Surveys (DHSs) and Living Standards Measurement Surveys (LSMSs), Multi-indicator Cluster Surveys (MICSs), the World Health Survey (WHS), other nationally developed and implemented surveys, and various government agencies (for example, ministries of energy and utilities). ### Overview This dataset shows energy intensity in 259 countries from 1990 to 2015. Energy intensity indicates how much primary energy (energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form) is used to produce one unit of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within an area. Energy intensity is expressed as megajoules (MJ) of primary energy available per GDP produced, based on [purchasing power parity (PPP)](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/ppp.htm) in 2011 U.S. dollars (USD). PPP is a factor used to convert local currencies to one comparable unit of measure based on the local cost of goods and services in each country. Low energy intensity is desirable, as it means that less energy is used to produce one more unit of economic output. Having a low energy intensity indicates that a country can increase its economic growth without having to rely as heavily on energy consumption. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative. The database is intended to help policymakers in government, business, and civil society work toward doubling the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology Energy intensity was measured as the ratio of total primary energy supply to the value added to the economy. Primary energy supply data came from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database. The value added to the economy was expressed in 2011 USD, adjusted for PPP. The data for GDP PPP came from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://trackingsdg7.esmap.org/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/431f7c9e-7ef5-4f00-a5dc-8845fcb3a9a9) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database.
