### Overview This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to conflict worldwide each year. Internal displacement refers to the forced movement of people within the country they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from conflict can include, but are not limited to - families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats; and - families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs. Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement. This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis. ### Methodology After IDMC learns that displacement due to conflict has occurred, it conducts situational monitoring within certain countries. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The UN Development Programme (UNDP) compiles the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) as part of its Human Development Report initiative. First published in 2010, the MPI identifies multiple deprivations at the household level in health, education, and standard of living. It uses microdata from household surveys, and—unlike the Inequality-Adjusted Human Development Index—all the indicators needed to construct the measure must come from the same survey. Each person in a given household is classified as poor or nonpoor depending on the weighted number of deprivations his or her household experiences. These data are then aggregated into the national measure of poverty. The MPI reflects both the prevalence of multidimensional deprivation and its intensity—the percentage of simultaneous deprivations poor people experience. It can be used to create a comprehensive picture of people living in poverty and permits comparisons both across countries, regions, and the world and within countries by ethnic group, urban, or rural location, as well as other key household and community characteristics. The MPI offers a valuable complement to income-based poverty measures. Indicators shown in the MPI include the following: (1) health: nutrition and child mortality; (2) education: years of schooling and children enrolled; and (3) standard of living: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets. The MPI is calculated by multiplying the incidence of poverty by the intensity of poverty. The incidence of poverty is the proportion of people considered to experience multidimensional poverty, in other words, that are considered deprived in at least one-third of the MPI's weighted indicators. The intensity of multidimensional poverty is the weighted average number of deprivations poor people experience at the same time. The main data sources of the MPI are the Macro Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of the Inner City Fund (ICF) and the Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS) of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). The 2020 Human Development Report (HDR) presents estimates for 107 countries—28 low income, 76 middle income, and 3 high income—and 5.9 billion people in developing regions. About 1.3 billion people in the 107 developing countries covered—22% of their entire population—lived in multidimensional poverty. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: ### Overview The Positive Peace Index (PPI) is a quantitative approach to measure Positive Peace. Positive Peace is defined as the attitudes, institutions, and structures that lead to a more peaceful society. A country with a higher PPI is more capable of building and maintaining peace. The Positive Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure a country’s success in building and maintaining peace. Positive peace is used to create resilient and adaptive communities that prevent conflict and help societies channel disagreements productively. The framework for PPI is based on eight domains: 1. *Acceptance of the Rights of Others:* This requires countries to have formal laws that can guarantee basic human rights and freedoms, ensure gender equality, and worker’s rights. 2. *Equitable Distribution of Resources:* This ensures everyone has equal access to resources, such as education and health. 3. *Free Flow of Information:* This is measured by the extent to which citizens can gain access to information, whether the media is free and independent, and how well-informed citizens are. 4. *Good Relations with Neighbours:* A country’s relationship with other countries is an important indicator of how peaceful and politically stable the country is. 5. *High Levels of Human Capital:* The employment rate among young citizens and the number of people engaged in research activities shows the level of social capital in a country. 6. *Low Levels of Corruption:* High levels of corruption leads to a shortage of funding for essential services, which creates unrest in a society. 7. *Sound Business Environment:* This is measured by the presence of regulatory systems and formal institutions in a country to support a good business environment. 8. *Well-Functioning Government:* A government that delivers high-quality public and civil services, creates trust and participation, maintains political stability, and promotes the rule of law is necessary for a peaceful country. The PPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2009 to 2018 for 163 countries covering 99.6% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand and make progress towards global peacefulness along with other interrelated areas such as: improved economic productivity and social advancement. ### Methodology The Positive Peace Index (PPI) uses 24 indicators in eight domains to measure Positive Peace. The eight domains range from the flow of information within a country to levels of corruption. PPI is interconnected to the Global Peace Index (GPI) which is another measurement for global peacefulness. GPI is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence in a country. The internal measures of the Global Peace Index were statistically compared to approximately 25,000 national data series, indices, and attitudinal surveys to determine the initial set of indicators for Positive Peace Index. These indicators were then qualitatively assessed. If there were multiple indicators for similar cases, the least important ones were discarded. Finally, the remaining indicators were aggregated into the eight domains of Positive Peace and given a correlation coefficient to their value in GPI using statistical approaches. The correlation coefficient represented how important the indicators were in the PPI measurement compared to GPI. The correlation coefficient was used to weight GPI Internal Peace scores for each indicator and create a final score out of 5. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/10/PPR-2019-web.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_092_positive_peace_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

### Overview The Cruise Ports dataset shows the number of visitors received by ports worldwide from July 2009 - June 2010. This dataset is part of the [Reefs at Risk Revisited](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited) report from World Resources Institute (WRI). Cruise port and passenger volume data was provided to WRI by [Clean Cruising](https://www.cleancruising.com.au/), a commercial cruise booking company based in Brisbane, Australia. Cruise ships can be a significant source of air and water pollution. According to a 2010 report from [Cruise Lines International Association](https://cruising.org/en/), a typical one-week cruise on a large ship (3,000 passengers and crew) generates almost 800 cubic meters of sewage; 3,700 cubic meters of graywater; half a cubic meter of hazardous waste; 8 tons of solid waste; and nearly 100 cubic meters of oily bilge water. Pollution from cruise ships can threaten coral reef health, particularly in the Atlantic where there are a large number of cruise ship ports. Cruise ships also produce harmful greenhouse gas emissions and can disturb marine wildlife. These problems are exacerbated in ports where several ships are frequently docked. Identifying locations and volume of cruise ship passengers can provide insight on where to expect environmental impacts to water and air quality at ports. The Cruise Ports dataset can also help inform environmental policy decisions in areas that receive high volumes of cruise ship passengers. The Cruise Ports dataset was provided by [WRI](https://www.wri.org/about), an independent, non-governmental global research organization that seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. WRI was founded in 1982 to address the environmental issues of deforestation, desertification and climate change. They use a science and evidence-based approach to achieve global change. WRI conducts independent research, tests ideas with leaders of cities, companies and countries, and implements proven ideas to transform societies and economies. ### Methodology The Cruise Ports dataset was generated by cruise port and passenger volume data provided by Clean Cruising. Passenger volume data was compiled from booking and departure information for all major cruise lines between July 2009 - June 2010. Port locations were mapped using the [National Geospatial Intelligence Agency World Port Index](https://msi.nga.mil/Publications/WPI.0). The Cruise Ports dataset was part of the Reefs at Risk Revisited report from WRI. For the full documentation, please see the source [technical documentation](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Global Oil Pipelines data set was assembled by Professor Jeff Blossom of Harvard University's Center for Geographic Analysis for a workshop in 2009. It gives a partial view of installed crude oil, natural gas, and petroleum product pipeline infrastructure as of August 2009. It covers the entire globe. The lines may not exactly match up with actual pipeline coordinates in some areas, as there was uncertainty in the source maps. Pipelines are snapped to source cities, and the paths between cities are slightly stylized while maintaining the general trend of each pipeline's path. Esri's ArcGIS tool was used to georeference pipeline data from Theodora.com's pipeline maps: http://www.theodora.com/pipelines/. These maps were in turn assembled from a variety of different sources. According to the Theodora site, no claims are made regarding the accuracy of the world pipelines data. Not all pipelines contained in Theodora maps were transferred to this map. ### Overview The Gender Gap Index quantifies the gaps between women and men in four key areas: health, education, economy, and politics. Data is available from 149 countries for select years between 2010-2021. Scores are based on the level of access women have to resources and opportunities relative to men. Countries are given a score from 0-1. A score of 1 indicates full equality between women and men and a score of 0 indicates full inequality. The Gender Gap Index is published annually by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and is designed to capture the magnitude of gender-based disparities and track progress over time. Gender equality is a necessity for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable world. Women represent half of the world’s population but continue to be underrepresented in leadership and in the workplace. According to the 2021 Gender Gap Index, only 27% of global managerial positions were held by women in 2021. The largest gap between women and men was in political empowerment, where only 26.1% of about 35,500 parliament seats and 22.6% of over 3,400 ministers globally are held by women. The Gender Gap Index serves as a benchmark for comparing countries and their progress to gender equality over time. Based on current trends, the WEF estimates that it will take 135.6 years to close the global gender gap. However, the 2021 Gender Gap Index shows that many countries have made significant progress towards closing the gender gap. These countries include Iceland, Finland, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Namibia, Rwanda, and Lithuania. The WEF Centre for the New Economy and Society published the Gender Gap Index. The WEF is an international NGO founded in 1971. Focused on public-private cooperation, the WEF brings together political, business and cultural leaders at their annual meetings, workshops and seminars. The WEF’s primary aim is to drive positive change for the world by conducting research, producing data and leading collaborative projects and initiatives. The Centre for the New Economy and Society is focused on closing economic gender gaps, fostering diversity and promoting inclusive growth. ### Methodology The Gender Gap Index quantified the gaps between men and women across four subindexes: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Indicators were scored within each subindex. The Gender Gap Index was based on three underlying concepts that determined how indicators were chosen, how the data was treated and how the index can be used. These concepts can be thought of as the “rules” for how the subindexes were scored. First, the index measured gender-based gaps in access to resources and opportunities in countries, rather than the actual levels of the available resources and opportunities. This rewarded countries with smaller gaps in access to these resources, regardless of the overall level of resources. Second, the index evaluated countries based on outcomes rather than inputs. Inputs – indicators related to country-specific policies, rights or customs – were not included in the index. For example, the gap between women and men in high-skilled jobs (an outcome indicator) was measured, but the length of maternity leave (a country-specific policy) was not. Third, the index evaluated countries based on their proximity to gender equality, rather than their level of women’s empowerment. The index rewarded countries in which outcomes for women equaled those for men, but it neither rewarded nor penalized countries in which women outperformed men. The four subindexes were scored based on the following indicators: - Economic participation and opportunity: This subindex measured gender-based gaps in workforce participation, remuneration and advancement. The remuneration gap was measured by the ratio of estimated female-to-male earned income and a qualitative assessment of wage equality for similar work. The advancement gap was captured through two hard data statistics: the ratio of women to men among legislators, senior officials and managers, and the ratio of women to men among technical and professional workers. Data was provided by the [International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) and the WEF. - Educational attainment: Gender-based gaps in educational attainment were measured with the ratio of women to men enrolled in primary, secondary and tertiary education. The ratio of female to male literacy was also used as an indicator of a country’s long-term ability to educate women and men. Data was provided by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Institute for Statistics Education Indicators database](http://uis.unesco.org/). - Health and survival: The differences between women’s and men’s health were measured using the sex ratio at birth and the gap between women’s and men’s healthy life expectancy. Sex ratio at birth is the measure of male births for every female birth and was included to capture the phenomenon of [“missing women.”](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/where-are-all-the-women/) This refers to the observation of a low ratio of women to men, particularly in countries with a strong son preference. Data for this subindex was provided by the [United Nations (UN) World Population Prospects dataset](https://population.un.org/wpp/) and the [World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Observatory database](https://www.who.int/data/gho). - Political empowerment: The gap between women and men at the highest level of political decision-making was measured by the ratio of women to men in ministerial positions and the ratio of women to men in parliamentary positions. The ratio of women to men in terms of years in executive office (prime minister or president) for the last 50 years was also included. Data was provided by the Inter-Parliamentary Union [Women in National Parliaments](http://archive.ipu.org/wmn-e/classif.htm). [Women in Politics](https://www.ipu.org/resources/publications/infographics/2020-03/women-in-politics-2020) datasets and the WEF. All data was converted to female-to-male ratios. Ratios were then truncated at the “equality benchmark”. The equality benchmark was 1 for all indicators except the two in the health subindex. The sex ratio at birth equality benchmark was 0.9445 and the healthy life expectancy benchmark was 1.06. Truncating ratios at 1 assigns the same score to a country that has reached equality between women and men (a ratio of 1) and one in which women have surpassed men (a ratio greater than 1). This method measured how close women were to achieving equality with men in a country, but did not reward or penalize countries with a gender gap in the opposite direction. The total score for each subindex was a weighted average of the scores for each indicator. A weighted average was used to make sure each indicator had the same relative impact on the total score.The overall score for each country was a simple average of the subindex scores. A score of 0 indicated complete inequality between women and men and a score of 1 indicated complete equality. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://reports.weforum.org/global-gender-gap-report-2018/measuring-the-global-gender-gap/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. As one of the four indicators in the Natural Resource Management Index, NRPI shows the degree to which a country protects at least 17% of terrestrial biome within its borders. It is computed as a standardized proximity-to-target ranging from 0 (worst performance) to 100 (at target or best performance). Biomes are broad ecological regions (e.g., a desert or deciduous forest). CIESIN utilized the 2016 World Database of Protected Areas (WDPA), ISciences coastline data set, and WWF's Terrestrial Ecoregions of the World data set (Olson et al. 2001) to compute the proportion of each biome in a country that is protected. The WDPA includes polygons that provide the actual boundaries of protected areas. The biome data, provided by the WWF data set, are manually matched with ISciences coastline data to ensure that all areas, particularly along the coast or small islands, are assigned a biome type. A composite layer consisting of all three data sets was created and the percentage of each biome that is protected was calculated. The percentage was capped at 17%, so that additional "credit" does not accrue where protection exceeds 17%. The countries' overall scores are a weighted average of the protection score for each biome. The weights are derived by calculating the biome area as a fraction of a country’s overall land area. Greater weights are applied to larger biomes. The indicator covers 237 countries and is updated based on the most recent monthly release of UNEP's World Conservation Monitoring WDPA. For more information, please see http://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/nrmi-natural-resource-protection-child-health-indicators-2016/docs Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

### Overview The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset estimates the share of household income that is spent on various types of products and services. Spending was analyzed for four consumption segments: lowest, low, middle, and higher. The four levels of consumption segments were based on income per capita: - Lowest: below $2.97 per capita a day - Low: between $2.97 and $8.44 per capita a day - Middle: between $8.44 and $23.03 per capita a day - Higher: above $23.03 per capita a day This dataset shows the percent of the household income that is spent on each type of product or service within each of these consumption segments. This dataset was developed by the World Bank Group as part of its Global Consumption Database. The data covers both urban and rural households in developing countries and is reported at the national level for the year 2010. ### Methodology The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset was developed using multiple different surveys, depending on data availability, including household budget survey, living standard measurement surveys, and various kinds of country-specific socioeconomic surveys. All surveys measure consumption at the household level; however, different surveys collected data over different time periods. Some conducted surveys over a period of 12 months to account for seasonality, while others collected data over a shorter period (a few weeks or a few months). Most surveys rely on the "recall method," in which households are asked to report what they can recall spending over a given period. The choice of recall period may have a significant impact on the level of consumption reported by the households. Data was collected for households in various developing countries. These households were categorized by their consumption segments for the Global Consumption Database. The consumption segments are based on the global income distribution data, which rank the global population by income per capita. The lowest consumption segment corresponds to the bottom half of the global distribution, or the 50th percentile and below; the low consumption segment to the 51st-75th percentiles; the middle consumption segment to the 76th-90th percentiles; and the higher consumption segments to the 91st percentile and above. The purchasing power parity (PPP) US dollar threshold was converted into annual expenditure in local currency (as of 2010). The Global Consumption Database draws on a diverse array of data surveys, so standardization was applied, to the extent possible, through a six-step process. The first step consisted of annualizing each household's consumption or expenditure data for each commodity. The second step was to detect and fix outliers. The third step was to map commodities found in each survey dataset to a standard classification of products and services. In the fourth step, extrapolations were done to convert all consumption and population data to a common reference year. In the fifth and sixth step, the resulting data was compared with data from other sources and used to generate a standard set of tables for each country showing consumption and demographic patterns across consumption segments. With the goal of producing information for decadal-scale planning, adaptation, and investment, the Aqueduct Water Stress Projections model potential changes in future demand and supply of water over the next 3 decades. Global indicators were developed for water demand (withdrawal and consumptive use), water supply, water stress (the ratio of water withdrawal to supply), and intra-annual (seasonal) variability for the periods centered on 2020, 2030, and 2040 for each of 2 climate scenarios, RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, and 2 shared socioeconomic pathways, SSP2 and SSP3. Estimates were derived from general circulation models (GCMs) from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and mixed-effects regression models based on projected socioeconomic variables from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis’s Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) database. This data set displays the rates of literacy per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics 2010 Population and Housing Census Report. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020. There are over 600 enumeration areas on the 3 main islands of Seychelles; this data set focuses on the enumeration areas on Mahé. Enumeration areas are composed of approximately 50-70 dwelling units each. The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households. The literacy rates were calculated by dividing the number of literate individuals in an enumeration area by the population of the respective enumeration area and converted to a percentage. This data represents the percentage of the population in each enumeration area that is classified as literate.

### Overview This dataset shows a global estimate of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans for 2010, expressed in kilograms per year. The authors used data on waste management, population density, and hydrological information to create this model. The dataset includes information on 40,760 watersheds and 182 different countries. The data is presented in a vector format. Plastic pollution in our oceans and on our coastlines have become a major threat to ocean health worldwide. A better understanding and quantification of marine plastic sources can help in implementing mitigation strategies to alleviate the issue. The dataset can help in identifying places that require higher attention in terms of plastic waste monitoring and mitigation plans. This data can also be used as a baseline measurement for ocean plastic mass balance exercises. This data was developed by researchers funded by The Ocean Cleanup Foundation. ### Methodology The amount of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans was estimated by using data on mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) per country, population density, topographic elevation, and location of artificial barriers (weirs and dams). For each catchment area mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) rates per day were calculated by combining data on waste generation by inhabitant per day and population density for the area. This data was combined with water flow per river catchment area to provide a final value for the mass of plastic released at the river’s mouth. This data was extrapolated using seasonal variations in water flow to create a year dataset. Data on population density was derived from the dataset Global 15 x 15 Minute Grids of the Downscaled Population by the Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) for 182 countries. Data used to calculate MPW rates were collected from seven peer reviewed studies. Topographic information was taken from Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) hydrological model for surface/subsurface runoff and location of artificial barriers was taken from AquaStat and Global Reservoir and Dam Database (GRanD). In total the dataset includes information for 40,760 watersheds worldwide. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15611#Sec6). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for plastic input in tonnes per year, plastic input in tonnes per month, and average monthly water runoff in catchment area in mm per day are also available from the data provider. ### Overview The Crop Land and Production dataset shows the global harvested area, production, and yield for six major crops: wheat, soybean, rice, maize, coffee, and cotton. The dataset was derived from the 2010 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and sub-national crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels, and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas, and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming. ### Methodology The main purpose of SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics (e.g., harvested area, production quantity, and yield) by different farming systems and to further allocate such disaggregated statistics into spatially gridded units. The whole procedure entails a data fusion approach that combines information from different sources and at different spatial scales by deploying various matching and calibration processes. Then all the data elements are processed by the optimization model, which generates results at the grid level. There are three submodules in a standardized SPAM model: disaggregation, optimization, and allocation. The SPAM2010 is conceptualized based on this general setting, while it adds further methodological and data improvements, which mainly include the update of base year, the expansion of subnational administrative-unit coverage, the extension of crop list, and the substitution of the latest hybrid cropland map as the basic allocation layer. The first step for SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics of agricultural production (e.g., the yield, harvested area, and total production) by administrative-unit levels (k), crop type (j), and farming system (l) from coarser scale to finer scale. The four production systems were defined by water and management type: - Irrigated – high input (I) - Rainfed – high input (H) - Rainfed – low input (L) - Rainfed – subsistence (S) The four conceptualized farming systems are mainly delineated by the water supply system and inputs used by farmers, despite global data on farming system shares for each crop being largely absent. For a small number of large countries, e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, the United States, the authors have data on farming system shares at the ADM1 level. For the other countries the authors assigned the national farming system shares to each ADM1 level and then adjusted individual ADM1 farming system shares in light of the supporting evidence. For irrigated farming systems, the crop-specific shares are derived by dividing the harvested area cultivated under full control irrigation obtained from [Global Information System on Water and Agriculture (AQUASTAT)](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/), [MIRCA](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GB003435), and country-level statistics by the overall harvested area. The optimization module in SPAM2010 is almost the same as that in previous versions. The authors applied a cross-entropy process in the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS), which ensures that the optimization procedure iterates until a solution is found. Once the allocation is successful, meaning that an optimal or locally optimal solution has been found, the routine immediately returns the allocated physical area by grid, crop and farming system, and the program continues with post-processing automatically. The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included (among several others): - Administrative units - Crop Type - Farming system - Adjusted harvested area - Total suitable area in each grid by crop and farming system - Crop prices - Market accessibility in each grid - Population density Our data catalog provides three of the SPAM2010 essential output indicators: - Harvested Area: also measured in hectares, harvested area is at least as large as physical area but sometimes more since it also accounts for multiple harvests of a crop on the same plot. Like for physical area, the harvested area is calculated for each production system, and the sum of all harvested areas of all production systems in a pixel amounts to the total harvested area of the pixel. The sum of all the harvested areas of the crops in a pixel can be larger than the pixel size. - Production: for each production system and crop, production is calculated by multiplying the area harvested by its corresponding yield. It is measured in metric tons. The total production of a crop includes the production of all production systems of that crop. - Yield: is the amount of production per harvested area and measured in kilograms per hectare. It is a measure of productivity. The total yield of a crop, when considering all production systems, is the weighted average of the four systems’ yields. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/3545/2020/essd-12-3545-2020.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2010 Version 2.0 has data for 36 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. This map of baseline water stress in major crop producing areas was created by WRI's Aqueduct program as part of the Water Risk Atlas, an online mapping tool that displays various aspects of water-related risks. The map displays the major crop producing areas for 13 major commodity crops (cocoa, coffee, cotton, maize, oats, oil palm, oranges, canola, rice, rubber, soybeans, sugarcane, and wheat) and 9 crop groups (cereals, fiber crops, fodder crops, fruits, oil crops, legumes, roots and tubers, sugar crops, and tree nuts), and the levels of water stress (low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high) experienced in these major crop-producing areas. Baseline water stress refers to the annual water withdrawals (municipal, industrial, and agricultural) expressed as a percentage of the total annual available flow. Higher values indicate more competition among users. Arid areas with low water use are shown in gray but scored as high stress when calculating aggregated scores. Baseline water stress is calculated by dividing water withdrawals (2010) by mean available blue water (1950-2008). Areas with available blue water and water withdrawal less than 0.03 and 0.012/m2 respectively are coded as “arid and low water use." Crop production in each category is computed by overlaying gridded crop production data, which was pulled from 2 articles in Global Biogeochemical Cycle (2008), "Farming the Planet: 1. Geographic Distribution of Global Agricultural Lands in the Year 2000" and "Farming the Planet: 2. Geographic Distribution of Crop Areas, Yields, Physiological Types, and Net Primary Production in the Year 2000." The authors of these studies identified croplands and crop production using a high-resolution satellite-derived land cover data set and agricultural inventory data to derive a global map of croplands. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

We recommend using [this dataset](c66d7f3a-d1a8-488f-af8b-302b0f2c3840) as a replacement.**_ In response to growing concerns from private sector actors around water availability, water quality, climate change, and increasing demand, World Resources Institute developed Aqueduct Global Maps to help decision-makers identify areas with higher exposure to water-related risks. Aqueduct employs the composite index approach as a robust communication tool to translate hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risks. 12 indicators were grouped into a framework identifying spatial variation in water risks for 15,006 subcatchments. The 12 global indicators (baseline water stress, interannual variability, seasonal variability, flood occurrence, drought severity, upstream storage, groundwater stress, return flow ratio, upstream protected land, media coverage, access to water, and threatened amphibians) were grouped into 3 categories of risk (physical quantity, quality, and regulatory and reputational risk) and 1 overall score. For 6 of the 12 indicators, an ensemble of time series estimators, spatial regression, and a sparse hydrological model was used to generate novel data sets of water supply and use. The remaining 6 indicators were adapted from existing publications. Aggregation methods were chosen to maximize transparency and communicability, and to allow for dynamic weighting to reflect different users’ sensitivities to water-related risks. Catchments with less than 0.012 m/m²/year of withdrawal and 0.03 m/m²/year of available blue water were masked out as “arid and low water use.” Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Gridded Livestock of the World Version 3, produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the University of Oxford, shows the distribution of eight livestock animal densities in animals per square kilometer at a spatial resolution of 5 arcminutes. The animals include cattle, water buffalo, horse, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and ducks. The Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW) created two versions of their data for two different methods of distributing livestock census weighting: area weighting and dasymetric weighting. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data, and the metadata refers to this methodology. More information can be found in the Cautions section. The total livestock census numbers for administrated levels are found by mining agricultural yearbooks or through direct contacts with ministries or statistical bureau. The livestock numbers are then distributed within census polygons according to weights established by a Random Forest model using high resolution spatial covariates including population, vegetation health, and climate. In compiling subnational census counts, priority is given to censuses that most closely match the reference year, 2010, and those with the highest level of spatial detail. This results in a global mosaic of data from different spatial resolutions and different years. Both the spatial resolution and year of census data depend on the country and species in question. See cautions section and source publication for more information. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The Oil Palm Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and the Solomon Islands. Concession name, company and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Oil Palm Concessions dataset. Oil Palm Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset is updated monthly. Palm oil is an edible vegetable oil produced from the fruits of the oil palm tree. According to the [World Wildlife Fund (WWF)](https://www.worldwildlife.org/industries/palm-oil), oil palm is a highly productive crop and grows only in tropical regions. Palm oil does not require refrigeration and is used in food products, cosmetics and detergents. However, oil palm farming contributes to deforestation and the release of harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. [According to a study from the European Commission](http://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/14868/), oil palm farming is responsible for 8% of global agriculture-related deforestation. Deforestation from oil palm farming is most prevalent in Indonesia, Brazil and Malaysia. Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of oil palm plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near real-time. This information is critical to ending illegal deforestation and fires, and promoting sustainable practices. It can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming. Additionally, farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources. ### Methodology The term “oil palm concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. GFW generated the Oil Palm Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and Solomon Islands. Most locations in the dataset include the company, concession name and concession area (ha). Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies and public documents. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. Data from the public domain (company websites, news reports, NGOs) was used for countries where data was not readily available from government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information such as company and concession name was added to the polygons as attributes. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=oilpalm). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset shows the projected inundation depth for river basins around the world, in a business as usual climate scenario. In this dataset, the inundation depth represents the depth of water over normally dry ground that would occur during 100-year floods. Inundation depths are calculated for the baseline year 2010 and predicted for future years 2030, 2050, and 2080. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 km x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Flooding is likely to intensify in the coming decades due to climate change. It is among the most serious of all global risks, causing loss of life and damage to property, livelihoods, and economies. As urbanization and economic growth put more people and assets into flood-prone areas, it is important to calculate flood risks and hazards around the world. However, these hazards are usually underestimated due to lack of data and information. This dataset helps change that by providing high resolution inundation depth data. The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset was created by the World Resource Institute (WRI) to assist in creating water use policies and assessing flood risks. This dataset is part of WRI’s Aqueduct datasets. Aqueduct helps to identify and evaluate water risks around the world. ### Methodology The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset was created using a Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) framework. GLOFRIS combines a global hydrological model called PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB) with river and floodplain routing scheme to make long-term simulations of river discharges and flood levels for a variety of climate conditions. In addition, meteorological datasets from European Water and Global Change (EUWATCH) were used to force PCR-GLOBWB over various time periods. Floodplain water volumes were then calculated using the PCR-GLOBWB outputs for a 2010 baseline, along with future climate scenarios in 2030, 2050, and 2080. The output flood volumes were converted to high resolution inundation maps using a volume spreading flood model. The “Riverine” hazard represents flooding from river overflow and occurs in river basins with an area of at least 10,000 kilometers squared. However, smaller floods do occur more regularly than larger floods. The data on Resource Watch shows what a 100-year flood (1% probability of occurrence per year) will look like for the selected years (2030, 2050, and 2080). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The map (v1.2) depicts the global extent of mangrove forests for the year 2010, derived by Random Forest Classification of both L-band radar (ALOS PALSAR) and optical (Landsat-5, -7) data. All satellite data and software used to derive the GMW mangrove maps are available in the public domain. The mangrove habitat definition was based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on a randomly sample of 38 million points using the mangrove masks (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for the establishment of fast-growing tree plantations to produce timber for paper and paper products. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from the Republic of the Congo, Indonesia and Malaysia. Concession name, group and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Wood Fiber Concessions dataset. Wood Fiber Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. Wood fiber is a cellulose material extracted from trees and converted to wood pulp to make paper products. These products include paper, paperboard, cardboard and tissue. The year-round growing season and low cost of business has made tropical regions a popular wood fiber growing location. In these areas, it is common practice to clear land and plant fast-growing trees like the acacia. [Studies have shown](https://www.wri.org/blog/2017/07/drivers-deforestation-indonesia-inside-and-outside-concessions-areas) that these practices contribute to deforestation and [destruction of carbon-rich peat soils](https://www.wri.org/blog/2018/01/save-indonesias-carbon-rich-peatlands-start-mapping-them). Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of wood fiber plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute (WRI)](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near-real-time. Understanding when and where deforestation is occurring is critical for ending illegal deforestation, fires, and unsustainable practices. Farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources. Additionally, this data can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming. ### Methodology The term “wood fiber concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale fast-growing timber plantations. GFW generated the Wood Fiber Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Republic of the Congo, Indonesia and Malaysia. Most locations in the dataset include the concession name, group and area (ha). Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies, environmental impact assessments and non-profits. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information, such as concession name and area, was added to the polygons as attributes. The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=wood%20fiber). We recommend using [this dataset](47053e23-7808-40d9-b4ae-1af73c5c8bab) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating for countries and water basins at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available water and estimates the degree to which freshwater availability is an ongoing concern in a region. The dataset’s main focus is to include detailed and accurate information for the world’s 100 most populous river basins, as they are often areas where water stress is a large concern. Additionally, researchers grouped the final dataset into water usage by different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand where water stress in an area is coming from. The dataset was calculated by comparing weighted averages of water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high. Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments creating water use policies. ### Methodology Researchers created this global dataset to include the 100 most populous river basins and all countries. Baseline water stress was calculated by dividing the weighted average water withdrawals in a region by the total blue freshwater available. To create the weighted average water withdrawals researchers used information on water withdrawals and divided each region into grid cells. Each grid cell was given a different weight based on the water withdrawals and water available within it. The grid cells were then combined to encompass different regions shown in the final dataset. Researchers further separated the dataset to view water usage in three different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial). Baseline water stress values were grouped into five categories when mapped: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high. The water stress scores for each category are as follows: Low <1, low to medium 1-5, medium to high 5-10, high 10-20, and extremely high >20. Each category represents the risk of water stress in the area. Data for country boundaries was taken from the Natural Earth Data 10m Admin 0 – Countries dataset. Data on the extent of the 100 most populous river basins was taken from HydroSHEDS 30s Basin Outlines and Gridded Population of the World, v3, Future Estimates 2010 datasets. Gridded weights and source indicators (baseline water stress) were calculated using Aqueduct Global Maps 2.0. The final dataset was created in tabular format and projected on a global map of the earth at a national scale. We recommend using [this dataset](2a571044-1a31-4092-9af8-48f406f13072) as a replacement.**_ With the goal of producing information for decadal-scale planning, adaptation, and investment, the Aqueduct Water Stress Projections model potential changes in future demand and supply of water over the next 3 decades. Global indicators were developed for water demand (withdrawal and consumptive use), water supply, water stress (the ratio of water withdrawal to supply), and intra-annual (seasonal) variability for the periods centered on 2020, 2030, and 2040 for each of 2 climate scenarios, RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, and 2 shared socioeconomic pathways, SSP2 and SSP3. Estimates were derived from general circulation models (GCMs) from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and mixed-effects regression models based on projected socioeconomic variables from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis’s Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) database. ### Overview The Global Croplands and Watering Source dataset shows the global distribution of irrigated and rainfed cropland, created through remote sensing data, secondary data (e.g. precipitation and elevation), and field data. The dataset displays the watering source (irrigation or rainfall) in areas where croplands are located. Irrigated cropland is cropland that is artificially watered through methods such as flooding fields or using sprinklers. Rainfed cropland refers to cropland that relies on rainfall for watering. The dataset is displayed at a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km). Identifying and monitoring global croplands and their water use is necessary in ensuring food security for the world’s growing population. According to [Global Croplands](https://croplands.org/home), 80% of abstracted freshwater is used on croplands. By understanding where and how this water is used, we can identify ways to better manage water resources for food production. In addition, according to the [U.S. Department of Agriculture](https://www.climatehubs.usda.gov/croplands-changing-climate), changing climate conditions are likely to affect water resources. Precipitation patterns, river flows, and groundwater availability can all change with shifting climate conditions, increasing food insecurity. Knowing how different regions water their croplands can be used in combination with climate change predictions to understand which areas may be impacted in the future. The Global Croplands and Watering Source dataset was created as part of a National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)-funded project that focused on overcoming traditional limitations from cropland data. These limitations include absence of crop types, coarse resolutions, and a lack of precise spatial locations. The project’s overarching goal is to produce accurate and unbiased cropland data. ### Methodology The Global Croplands and Watering Source dataset was derived from four major sources: Biradar et al. ([2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0303243408000834?via%3Dihub)) and Thenkabail et al. ([2009a](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/9780429147173)), ([2011](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/e/9780429143687)) used a combination of data from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHHR) instrument and vegetation data from the Satellite Probatoire d'Observation de la Terre (SPOT) satellite, as well as numerous secondary data sources (e.g. precipitation, temperature, and elevation) to produce a global irrigated area map and a second global map of rainfed cropland areas. Pittman et al. ([2010](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/2/7/1844)) used data from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) 250 meter (m) satellite to develop a map featuring cropland extent throughout the world. Yu et al. ([2013](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17538947.2013.822574)) produced a nominal 30 m resolution cropland extent of the world. Friedl et al. ([2010](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0034425709002673) created a MODIS global land cover and land use map. Each map was resampled to a resolution of 1 km. Then data overlays were created to determine similarities and differences between the datasets. By aggregating these maps, five classes were produced: (0) Noncroplands; (1) Croplands, Irrigation major; (2) Croplands, Irrigation minor; (3) Croplands, Rainfed; (4) Croplands, Rainfed minor fragments; (5) Croplands, Rainfed very minor fragments. Irrigation major areas refer to cropland irrigated by large reservoirs created by large and medium dams, barrages, and even large groundwater pumping. Irrigation minor areas refer to cropland irrigated by small reservoirs, irrigation tanks, open wells, and other minor irrigation. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on crop type and cropping intensity can be found at the source. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Only grid cells where croplands are located are displayed on the Resource Watch map - non cropland areas are not shown. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: This data set displays the female share of the population per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics 2010 Population and Housing Census Report. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020. There are over 600 enumeration areas on the 3 main islands of Seychelles; this data set focuses on the enumeration areas on Mahé. Enumeration areas are composed of approximately 50-70 dwelling units each. The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households. The female share of the population was calculated by dividing the number of females in an enumeration area by the population of the respective enumeration area and converted into a percentage. This data represents the percentage of the population in each enumeration area that identifies as female.

The Aqueduct Global Flood Risk Maps measures river flood impacts by urban damage, affected GDP, and affected population at the country, state, and river basin scale across the globe, as well as 120 cities. The maps estimate current flood risk for a specific geographic unit, taking into account existing local flood protection levels. They project future flood risk with three climate and socio-economic change scenarios. For the current scenario, hydrological data from 1960 through 1999 were used for generating flood inundations for 9 return periods, from 2-year flood to 1000-year flood, and 2010 GDP, population, and land use data for assessing flood impacts. For future projections, the following scenarios were used: 5 GCMs (Global Climate Models) from CMIP5 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5) projecting future flood inundations under two climate scenarios, RCP4.5 (Representative Concentration Pathway) and RCP8.5, and projected socio-economic changes using SSP2 (Shared Socio-economic Pathway) and SSP3, from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Assessment Report 5. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

The Gridded Livestock of the World Version 3, produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the University of Oxford, shows the distribution of eight livestock animal densities in animals per square kilometer at a spatial resolution of 5 arcminutes. The animals include cattle, water buffalo, horse, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and ducks. The Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW) created two versions of their data for two different methods of distributing livestock census weighting: area weighting and dasymetric weighting. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data, and the metadata refers to this methodology. More information can be found in the Cautions section. The total livestock census numbers for administrated levels are found by mining agricultural yearbooks or through direct contacts with ministries or statistical bureau. The livestock numbers are then distributed within census polygons according to weights established by a Random Forest model using high resolution spatial covariates including population, vegetation health, and climate. In compiling subnational census counts, priority is given to censuses that most closely match the reference year, 2010, and those with the highest level of spatial detail. This results in a global mosaic of data from different spatial resolutions and different years. Both the spatial resolution and year of census data depend on the country and species in question. See cautions section and source publication for more information. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

### Overview Coastal flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by coastal flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by coastal floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.0009‬%) to extremely high (>0.2%). Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by storm surge), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.” Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Data on the population impacted by coastal floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Coastal hazard maps were derived using Global Tide and Surge Reanalysis (GTSR) [(Muis et al., 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11969) datasets from 1974-2014.The coastal flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’x5’ (regridded to 30”x30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30”. Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the FLOPROS model. The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line. The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods. Finally, raw coastal flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw coastal flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0 to 9 in 1,000,000 people - Low to medium (1-2): 9 in 1,000,000 to 7 in 100,000 people - Medium to high (2-3): 7 in 100,000 to 3 in 10,000 people - High (3-4): 3 in 10,000 people to 2 in 1,000 people - Extremely high (4-5): > 2 in 1,000 people For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](386314c4-ab42-47a7-b2cd-596b788e114d) as a replacement.**_ This data set was generated by Aberystwyth University and soloEO within the framework of the Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) project, which is a part of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Kyoto and Carbon Initiative and the Mangrove Capital Africa Programme coordinated by Wetlands International and financed by DOB Ecology. The map (v1.2) depicts the global extent of mangrove forests for the year 2010, derived by Random Forest Classification of both L-band radar (ALOS PALSAR) and optical (Landsat-5, -7) data. All satellite data and software used to derive the GMW mangrove maps are available in the public domain. Approximately 15,000 Landsat scenes and 1,500 ALOS PALSAR (1 x 1 degree) mosaic tiles were used to create mosaics of optical and radar data covering the tropical, subtropical, and temperate coastlines of the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Oceania where mangroves occur. The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on a randomly sample of 38 million points using the mangrove masks (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c66d7f3a-d1a8-488f-af8b-302b0f2c3840) as a replacement.**_ In response to growing concerns from private sector actors around water availability, water quality, climate change, and increasing demand, World Resources Institute developed Aqueduct Global Maps to help decision-makers identify areas with higher exposure to water-related risks. Aqueduct employs the composite index approach as a robust communication tool to translate hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risks. 12 indicators were grouped into a framework identifying spatial variation in water risks for 15,006 subcatchments. The 12 global indicators (baseline water stress, interannual variability, seasonal variability, flood occurrence, drought severity, upstream storage, groundwater stress, return flow ratio, upstream protected land, media coverage, access to water, and threatened amphibians) were grouped into 3 categories of risk (physical quantity, quality, and regulatory and reputational risk) and 1 overall score. For 6 of the 12 indicators, an ensemble of time series estimators, spatial regression, and a sparse hydrological model was used to generate novel data sets of water supply and use. The remaining 6 indicators were adapted from existing publications. Aggregation methods were chosen to maximize transparency and communicability, and to allow for dynamic weighting to reflect different users’ sensitivities to water-related risks. Catchments with less than 0.012 m/m²/year of withdrawal and 0.03 m/m²/year of available blue water were masked out as “arid and low water use.” Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview Riverine flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by riverine flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by riverine floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.1%) to extremely high (>1%). Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by river overflow), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.” Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Data on the population impacted by riverine floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Riverine hazard maps were derived using PCR-GLOBWB 2 inputs from 1960-1999. The riverine flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’ x 5’ (regridded to 30” x 30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30". Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the [FLOPROS model](https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-16-1049-2016). The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line. The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods. Finally, raw riverine flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw riverine flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0 to 1 in 1,000 people - Low to medium (1-2): 1 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000 people - Medium to high (2-3): 2 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000 people - High (3-4): 6 in 1,000 people to 1 in 100 people - Extremely high (4-5): > 1 in 100 people For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.
